1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Four Knights Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.background: Popular among the Open Games in the nineteenth century, the Four Knights had lost ground by the First World War, and it saw a renaissance in the 1990s, since when grandmasters have played it again.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards e5 and asks Black to react. Unlike in the Ruy Lopez, the c3 knight takes the square from White's c-pawn, so there is no broad pawn centre to build, and the game stays even and manoeuvring rather than sharp.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.background: With 4.d4, one of the two most common continuations of the Four Knights Game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, castle and build up slowly. It leads to a less drawish game than most of the Four Knights, but Black can equalise with a sound central strike.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.name: Four Knights Game: Glek System
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.background: A modern try advocated by Igor Glek.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: White removes Black's e-pawn and develops with space and open lines, with the knight already on c3. It is more direct than the quiet lines, but Black develops easily.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.background: With 4.Bb5, one of the two most common continuations of the Four Knights Game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it takes b4 from Black's bishop and passes the turn, hoping for a Four Knights with colours reversed. It develops nothing, so Black can simply take the centre.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.name: Four Knights Game: Gunsberg Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.background: A specialty of the Polish grandmaster Paweł Blehm.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.strategy: Leaves the e4 pawn undefended on purpose. A Black knight that grabs it wins a pawn or two, but White gets an active position with traps for the unwary; calm development is the safer way to meet it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.name: Four Knights Game: Naroditsky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.background: A blitz favourite of Daniel Naroditsky. After his death Hikaru Nakamura played it in memoriam against Magnus Carlsen and called for the line to be known by his name.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.strategy: Gives a knight for a pawn in the hope of a lead in development and a pawn centre that drives Black's knights back. Black simply takes the knight, keeps the extra piece and can return it on good terms, so the compensation is not enough.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.name: Four Knights Game: Halloween Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.background: In 1888 Oskar Cordel reported that Leipzig club players used the gambit to dangerous effect; their name for it, the Müller–Schulze Gambit, was a joke in German and did not refer to any real players. The modern name was given by the German player Steffen Jakob, who compared the shock of facing it when prepared for a boring Four Knights to being frightened by a Halloween mask.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6.strategy: A solid reply that guards e5 and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, keeping the position symmetrical. It is a little passive: claiming the centre with a pawn is the more ambitious way to punish the waiting move.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and eyes the c3 knight that guards e4, so Black's pressure matches White's. The position stays symmetrical and solid, a game of manoeuvring in which neither side has an easy edge: the most reliable way to meet the Spanish bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4.strategy: An unbalancing counterattack: instead of defending c6, the knight moves to d4 and hits the bishop and the f3 knight at once. It leaves e5 loose, but taking it is not as easy as it looks, and Black plays for activity over safety.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bc5.strategy: The classical set-up: the bishop develops towards f2 and gives Black a tactical defence of e5, since taking on c6 and then e5 runs into a strike at f2. The price is a more open game in which White can choose between quiet and sharp play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 a6.strategy: Borrows the Ruy Lopez question, but here the c3 knight already guards e4, so White can take on c6 and go after e5. Black has to rely on a forcing tactic to regain the pawn, which makes this a less natural choice than the mirror moves.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn with tempo, as the capture attacks the c3 knight at once. The centre opens and White has to recover the pawn or move the knight, while Black accepts an open game with no weaknesses of its own.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3 knight against the king, so that e4 loses its defender and Black threatens to take it. The cost is the e5 pawn, which is attacked twice and defended once: White can simply take it, and Black has to prove that the pin and the pressure on e4 pay for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once: e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and the f6 knight and defended only by the c3 knight, so White has to resolve the tension. Black claims a share of the centre and reaches an equal game, which takes the sting out of the fianchetto plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the knight: Black is a piece up for a pawn and White's compensation is a lead in development. Accepting is the critical reply, since it puts the extra material to the test and leaves White to prove the attack.
